newsitem.title: USA: GDP figure may understate U.S. performance -- experts.
newsitem.headline: GDP figure may understate U.S. performance -- experts.

text.p: A persistent gap between two key measurements of the U.S. economy's overall growth released earlier this week puzzles government economists charged with reconciling them.

What worries them is that according to official figures, real gross domestic product (GDP), which measures the total output of the economy, recently appears to have grown less vigorously than gross domestic income (GDI), the money earned from selling that output.
"We're quite concerned," Commerce economist Larry Morgan told Reuters. "We're taking steps to see whether we can locate the source of the discrepancy."

The Commerce Department said on Thursday that GDP grew by an annualized 2.9 percent over the past four years, while GDI grew at a real 3.4 percent. The difference translates into some $60 billion in real money, suggesting that the economy may actually have done even better than the widely-watched GDP figures indicate.

Allen Sinai, chief global economist at Boston-based Primark Decision Economics Inc. said while the size of the gap had narrowed slightly in the second quarter, the reason for its continued existence was still a mystery.
"It's disappointing that the discrepancy did not get reconciled. Income is still rising much faster than product and the puzzle is what does it mean and why," he said.
A GDP figure that may have understated actual growth and productivity gains over the past few years could have sent the wrong signals to both policy makers and financial markets.
Commerce undersecretary Lee Price earlier on Thursday told reporters the size and persistence of the gap was "unusual" and that it was a "very high priority" to realign the two measures.
One of the key dangers of not having an accurate way to measure output is that you may miss the key moment at which expansion begins to turn either to decline or to overheating.
That would be particularly worrying for the Federal Reserve, which insists it must act pre-emptively to keep the economy on an even keel.
But while it may be an imperfect measure, most observers agree that GDP is still the best gauge of economic activity.
"It may be a crooked game, but its the only game in town," said David Wyss of Massachusetts-based DRI/McGraw-Hill.

Experts say the key weakness of GDI is that it relies heavily on Internal Revenue Service (IRS) tax receipts, details of which become available only with a considerable time-lag. That would make GDI an educated guess more than anything else.
"We have more confidence in the source data on the production side than in the source data on the income side," said Commerce's Moran.

Analysts say regardless of whether growth is half a percent higher or half a percent lower than thought, the bottom line is that the U.S. economy is enjoying a period of strong expansion and low inflation -- and that is what counts.
"You dont have to look at the data, just look at the car in your neighbour's driveway," said Wyss of DRI/McGraw-Hill. "Stop whining -- things are good!" ((-- Washington newsroom, 202 898 8377))
